subject: Climate & Environment
title: Predicting and Tracking Hurricanes
description: A quick win: understand Predicting and Tracking Hurricanes.

hook.text: In 1900, a hurricane killed 8,000 people in Galveston, Texas. Nobody saw it coming.

buildup.text: Today, satellites track storms from birth. Weather planes fly directly into the eye for data.

discovery.text: Computer models now predict a storm's track 5 days out with impressive accuracy.

twist.text: Predicting intensity is much harder. Storms can rapidly strengthen just before landfall.

climax.text: Better forecasts save thousands of lives through earlier evacuations and preparation.

punchline.text: We can't stop a hurricane. But we can see it coming — and that saves everything.

quiz.question: What aspect of hurricanes is hardest to predict?

details.summary: Modern hurricane forecasting uses weather satellites, aircraft reconnaissance, ocean buoys, and supercomputer models to predict storm paths 5 to 7 days in advance. Track forecasts have improved dramatically, but intensity prediction remains a major challenge.
details.whyItMatters: Accurate forecasts save lives by enabling evacuation and preparation. Understanding why intensity prediction lags behind track prediction highlights remaining scientific frontiers.
takeaways: Hurricane track forecasts have improved roughly 50 percent since 2000
Intensity prediction has improved far less than track forecasting
Hurricane hunter aircraft fly into storms to gather direct measurements

faq.question: How far in advance can we predict a hurricane's path?
faq.answer: Modern models provide useful track forecasts 5 to 7 days ahead, with 3-day forecasts now as accurate as 1-day forecasts were 30 years ago. Path errors average about 100 miles at 3 days, requiring large coastal evacuation zones.

faq.question: Why is hurricane intensity harder to predict than path?
faq.answer: Intensity depends on small-scale processes within the storm core, ocean heat content at depth, and internal dynamics that even high-resolution models struggle to capture. Rapid intensification before landfall remains especially difficult to forecast.
